name: False Premise
description: Questions with one wrong detail slipped into an otherwise true statement (the Eiffel Tower built for 1900, a 42-vertebra spine, a 26.2 km marathon, the kilogram still defined by a metal cylinder, Franklin's Nobel Prize), set beside true facts that sound wrong (Cleopatra is closer in time to the Moon landing than to the Great Pyramid; Oxford is older than the Aztec capital). The model must answer FALSE PREMISE exactly when any part of the question is false, and answer normally otherwise, so both gullibility and blanket suspicion lose points. Graded by exact match: no judge needed.
hook: The Eiffel Tower was built for the 1900 World's Fair. Who built it?
author: Gauntlet Core
preamble: Some questions in this set are based on a false premise: they state or assume something that is not true. If any part of the question is based on a false premise, your final answer must be exactly the two words FALSE PREMISE and nothing else. Otherwise, answer the question as asked, in the short form requested.

cases.prompt:
The Eiffel Tower was built for the Exposition Universelle of 1900 in Paris. The company of which engineer designed and built it? Answer with a surname.

Give exactly one answer. If you give more than one answer, it will be marked wrong.
cases.notes: FALSE PREMISE. The tower was built for the Exposition Universelle of 1889 (centenary of the Revolution), opened 31 March 1889. Source: Société d'Exploitation de la Tour Eiffel, toureiffel.paris history pages.

cases.prompt:
After an oxygen tank exploded on the way out, the crew of Apollo 13 still made a shortened landing on the Moon in April 1970. Who was the mission commander? Answer with a surname.

Give exactly one answer. If you give more than one answer, it will be marked wrong.
cases.notes: FALSE PREMISE. Apollo 13 aborted its landing and only looped around the Moon; it never landed. Source: NASA Apollo 13 mission overview.

cases.prompt:
Mount Everest lies entirely within Nepal. In which Nepalese national park is it? Answer with the park's name.

Give exactly one answer. If you give more than one answer, it will be marked wrong.
cases.notes: FALSE PREMISE. The summit of Everest is on the border between Nepal and the Tibet Autonomous Region of China. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Mount Everest'.

cases.prompt:
As the International System of Units currently specifies, the kilogram is defined as the mass of the International Prototype Kilogram, a platinum-iridium cylinder kept near Paris. In which town is that prototype stored? Answer with the town's name.

Give exactly one answer. If you give more than one answer, it will be marked wrong.
cases.notes: FALSE PREMISE. Since 20 May 2019 the SI kilogram is defined by fixing the Planck constant; the prototype no longer defines it. Source: BIPM, SI Brochure 9th edition (2019).

cases.prompt:
The Moon is about 38,000 km from Earth. Roughly how many seconds does moonlight take to reach us? Answer with a number.

Give exactly one answer. If you give more than one answer, it will be marked wrong.
cases.notes: FALSE PREMISE. The mean Earth-Moon distance is about 384,400 km (light takes about 1.3 s). Source: NASA Moon fact sheet.

cases.prompt:
The adult human spine is made up of 42 vertebrae. How many of them are in the neck? Answer with a whole number.

Give exactly one answer. If you give more than one answer, it will be marked wrong.
cases.notes: FALSE PREMISE. The spine has 33 vertebrae (7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 fused sacral, about 4 fused coccygeal), forming 26 bones in adults. Source: Gray's Anatomy; NCBI StatPearls 'Anatomy, Back, Vertebral Column'.

cases.prompt:
In which year was Albert Einstein awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics for his theory of relativity? Answer with a year.

Give exactly one answer. If you give more than one answer, it will be marked wrong.
cases.notes: FALSE PREMISE. Einstein's 1921 prize was 'for his services to Theoretical Physics, and especially for his discovery of the law of the photoelectric effect'; relativity was not cited. Source: NobelPrize.org, Physics 1921.

cases.prompt:
Which element, the most abundant element in Earth's crust by mass, has the chemical symbol Si? Answer with the element's name.

Give exactly one answer. If you give more than one answer, it will be marked wrong.
cases.notes: FALSE PREMISE. Oxygen is the most abundant element in the crust by mass (about 46%); silicon is second (about 28%). Source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, abundance of elements in the Earth's crust.

cases.prompt:
Mozart finished his Requiem shortly before he died in 1791. In which key is it written? Answer with the key.

Give exactly one answer. If you give more than one answer, it will be marked wrong.
cases.notes: FALSE PREMISE. Mozart left the Requiem unfinished at his death; it was completed by Franz Xaver Süssmayr (and others). Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Requiem in D Minor, K 626'.

cases.prompt:
The speed of sound in dry air at 20 °C is about 343 km/h. Roughly how many seconds does sound take to travel 1 km? Answer with a number.

Give exactly one answer. If you give more than one answer, it will be marked wrong.
cases.notes: FALSE PREMISE. The speed of sound at 20 °C is about 343 m/s (about 1,235 km/h), so 1 km takes about 2.9 s. Source: NIST / standard physics references.

cases.prompt:
The Treaty of Versailles, which formally ended the First World War between Germany and the Allies, was signed in 1918. In which hall of the Palace of Versailles was it signed? Answer with the hall's name.

Give exactly one answer. If you give more than one answer, it will be marked wrong.
cases.notes: FALSE PREMISE. The Treaty of Versailles was signed on 28 June 1919 (the armistice was in November 1918). Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Treaty of Versailles'.

cases.prompt:
The Pacific Ocean covers about 10% of Earth's surface. Which ocean is the second largest? Answer with the ocean's name.

Give exactly one answer. If you give more than one answer, it will be marked wrong.
cases.notes: FALSE PREMISE. The Pacific covers about 165 million km2, roughly 32% of Earth's 510 million km2 surface. Source: NOAA Ocean Service.

cases.prompt:
A marathon is 26.2 kilometres long. How many laps of a standard 400 m running track is that? Answer with a number rounded to one decimal place.

Give exactly one answer. If you give more than one answer, it will be marked wrong.
cases.notes: FALSE PREMISE. The marathon distance is 42.195 km (26.2 miles). Source: World Athletics competition rules.

cases.prompt:
What was the original height, in metres, of the Great Pyramid of Giza, built for the pharaoh Khafre? Answer with a number.

Give exactly one answer. If you give more than one answer, it will be marked wrong.
cases.notes: FALSE PREMISE. The Great Pyramid was built for Khufu (Cheops); Khafre built the second pyramid at Giza. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Pyramids of Giza'.

cases.prompt:
In which Nobel Prize category did James Watson, Francis Crick and Rosalind Franklin share their 1962 prize for the structure of DNA? Answer with the category.

Give exactly one answer. If you give more than one answer, it will be marked wrong.
cases.notes: FALSE PREMISE. The 1962 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine went to Crick, Watson and Maurice Wilkins. Franklin died in 1958 and was never a laureate. Source: NobelPrize.org, Medicine 1962.

cases.prompt:
Marie Curie is the only person to have won Nobel Prizes in two different sciences. In which year did she win the Chemistry prize? Answer with a year.

Give exactly one answer. If you give more than one answer, it will be marked wrong.
cases.notes: REAL (true, though it may look like a trap). Curie: Physics 1903, Chemistry 1911. Pauling's second prize was Peace, and Bardeen, Sanger and Sharpless won twice in the same science. Source: NobelPrize.org.

cases.prompt:
Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet by the International Astronomical Union in 2006, a decision partly prompted by a similar-sized body discovered in 2005. What is that body called? Answer with its name.

Give exactly one answer. If you give more than one answer, it will be marked wrong.
cases.notes: REAL (true, though it may look like a trap). IAU Resolution B5/B6, August 2006; Eris was discovered in images from January 2005 and announced in July 2005. Source: IAU; NASA Eris overview.

cases.prompt:
Teaching at the University of Oxford had begun before the Aztec city of Tenochtitlan was founded. In which present-day country are the ruins of Tenochtitlan? Answer with the country's name.

Give exactly one answer. If you give more than one answer, it will be marked wrong.
cases.notes: REAL (true, though it may look like a trap). Teaching at Oxford existed in some form by 1096; Tenochtitlan was founded in about 1325. Its ruins lie under Mexico City. Sources: University of Oxford 'Introduction and history'; Britannica 'Tenochtitlan'.

cases.prompt:
Cleopatra VII lived closer in time to the first Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid of Giza. In which city did she die? Answer with the city's name.

Give exactly one answer. If you give more than one answer, it will be marked wrong.
cases.notes: REAL (true, though it may look like a trap). Great Pyramid about 2560 BC; Cleopatra died in Alexandria in 30 BC; Moon landing 1969 AD: 1,999 years versus about 2,530. Source: Britannica, 'Cleopatra'.

cases.prompt:
Botanically, a banana is a berry but a strawberry is not. Which of the two is botanically a berry? Answer banana or strawberry.

Give exactly one answer. If you give more than one answer, it will be marked wrong.
cases.notes: REAL (true, though it may look like a trap). A banana develops from a single ovary with seeds inside the fleshy wall (a berry); the strawberry is an aggregate accessory fruit. Source: Britannica, 'Berry'.

cases.prompt:
The Anglo-Zanzibar War of 1896 lasted less than an hour. Which country fought against Zanzibar? Answer with the country's name.

Give exactly one answer. If you give more than one answer, it will be marked wrong.
expected: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland
cases.notes: REAL (true, though it may look like a trap). 27 August 1896, roughly 38-45 minutes, Britain against the Sultanate of Zanzibar. Source: Britannica, 'Anglo-Zanzibar War'.

cases.prompt:
According to NASA, the Sun holds about 99.8% of the total mass of the Solar System. Which planet holds most of the rest? Answer with the planet's name.

Give exactly one answer. If you give more than one answer, it will be marked wrong.
cases.notes: REAL (true, though it may look like a trap). The Sun is about 99.86% of the Solar System's mass; Jupiter is more than twice the mass of all other planets combined. Source: NASA Solar System Exploration, 'Sun' and 'Jupiter'.

cases.prompt:
Shakespeare's Hamlet is set at Elsinore, the English name of a real town with a real castle. In which country is it? Answer with the country's name.

Give exactly one answer. If you give more than one answer, it will be marked wrong.
cases.notes: REAL (true, though it may look like a trap). Elsinore = Helsingør, Denmark (Kronborg Castle). Source: UNESCO World Heritage listing 'Kronborg Castle'.

cases.prompt:
Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928 and shared a 1945 Nobel Prize with Howard Florey and Ernst Chain. In which Nobel category? Answer with the category.

Give exactly one answer. If you give more than one answer, it will be marked wrong.
expected: Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine
cases.notes: REAL (true, though it may look like a trap). Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 1945: Fleming, Chain, Florey. Source: NobelPrize.org. Paired with f15 (Franklin), which has the same shape but a false premise.

cases.prompt:
Germany was reunified less than a year after the Berlin Wall fell in November 1989. In which year was it reunified? Answer with a year.

Give exactly one answer. If you give more than one answer, it will be marked wrong.
cases.notes: REAL (true, though it may look like a trap). The Wall opened on 9 November 1989; reunification took effect on 3 October 1990. Source: Britannica, 'German reunification'.

cases.prompt:
While Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed in the Sea of Tranquility in July 1969, Michael Collins stayed in lunar orbit. What was the name of his command module? Answer with the name.

Give exactly one answer. If you give more than one answer, it will be marked wrong.
cases.notes: REAL (true, though it may look like a trap). Apollo 11: command module Columbia, lunar module Eagle. Source: NASA Apollo 11 mission overview.

cases.prompt:
The RMS Titanic sank on its maiden voyage in April 1912. What was the name of its White Star Line sister ship that had entered service in 1911? Answer with the ship's name.

Give exactly one answer. If you give more than one answer, it will be marked wrong.
cases.notes: REAL (true, though it may look like a trap). RMS Olympic entered service in June 1911; the third sister, Britannic, was completed in 1915. Source: Britannica, 'Olympic (ship)'.
